{{Short description|Array of nonnegative integers in combinatorics}}
[[File:BeispielPlanePartition.jpg|thumb|A plane partition of 30 represented as stacks of unit cubes]]

In [[mathematics]] and especially in [[combinatorics]], a '''plane partition''' is a two-dimensional array of nonnegative integers <math>\pi_{i,j}</math> (with [[positive number|positive]] [[integer]] indices ''i'' and ''j'') that is nonincreasing in both indices. This means that
:<math> \pi_{i,j} \ge \pi_{i,j+1}</math> and <math>\pi_{i,j} \ge \pi_{i+1,j}</math> for all ''i'' and ''j''.
Moreover, only finitely many of the <math>\pi_{i, j}</math> may be nonzero.  Plane partitions are a generalization of [[Partition (number theory)|partitions of an integer]].

A plane partition may be represented visually by the placement of a stack of <math>\pi_{i,j}</math> [[unit cube]]s above the point (''i'', ''j'') in the plane, giving a three-dimensional solid as shown in the picture. The image has matrix form

:<math> \begin{matrix}
4 & 4 & 3 & 2 & 1\\
4 & 3 & 1 & 1\\
3 & 2 & 1\\
1
\end{matrix}
</math>

Plane partitions are also often described by the positions of the unit cubes. From this point of view, a plane partition can be defined as a finite subset <math>\mathcal{P}</math> of positive [[integer lattice]] points (''i'', ''j'', ''k'') in <math>\mathbb{N}^3</math>, such that if (''r'', ''s'', ''t'') lies in <math>\mathcal{P}</math> and if <math>(i, j, k)</math> satisfies <math>1\leq i\leq r</math>, <math>1\leq j\leq s</math>, and <math>1\leq k\leq t</math>, then (''i'', ''j'', ''k'') also lies in <math>\mathcal{P}</math>.

The ''sum'' of a plane partition is
:<math> n=\sum_{i,j} \pi_{i,j} .</math>
The sum describes the number of cubes of which the plane partition consists.  Much interest in plane partitions concerns the [[enumeration]] of plane partitions in various classes.  The number of plane partitions with sum ''n'' is denoted by PL(''n'').  For example, there are six plane partitions with sum 3
:<math> \begin{matrix} 3 \end{matrix}
\qquad \begin{matrix} 2 & 1 \end{matrix}
\qquad \begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \end{matrix}
\qquad \begin{matrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{matrix}
\qquad \begin{matrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 \end{matrix}
\qquad \begin{matrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{matrix}
</math>
so PL(3) = 6.

Plane partitions may be classified by how symmetric they are.  Many symmetric classes of plane partitions are enumerated by simple product formulas.

== Generating function of plane partitions ==

The [[generating function]] for PL(''n'') is<ref>[[Richard P. Stanley]], ''Enumerative Combinatorics'', Volume 2.  Corollary 7.20.3.</ref>
:<math> \sum_{n=0}^\infty \operatorname{PL}(n) x^n = \prod_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(1-x^k)^k} = 1+x+3x^2+6x^3+13x^4+24x^5+\cdots\qquad</math>{{OEIS|id=A000219}}.
It is sometimes referred to as the ''MacMahon function'', as it was discovered by [[Percy Alexander MacMahon|Percy A. MacMahon]].

This formula may be viewed as the 2-dimensional analogue of [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]]'s [[Integer partition#Generating function|product formula]] for the number of [[Partition (number theory)|integer partitions]] of ''n''. There is no analogous formula known for partitions in higher dimensions (i.e., for [[solid partition]]s).<ref>[[Richard P. Stanley|R.P. Stanley]], ''Enumerative Combinatorics'', Volume 2.  pp. 365, 401–2.</ref> The asymptotics for plane partitions were first calculated by [[E. M. Wright]].<ref>[[E. M. Wright]], Asymptotic partition formulae I. Plane partitions, The Quarterly Journal of Mathematics '''1''' (1931) 177–189.</ref> One obtains, for large <math> n </math>, that{{efn|Here the typographical error (in Wright's paper) has been corrected, pointed out by Mutafchiev and Kamenov.<ref>L. Mutafchiev and E. Kamenov, "Asymptotic formula for the number of plane partitions of positive integers", Comptus Rendus-Academie Bulgare Des Sciences '''59''' (2006), no. 4, 361.</ref>}}
:<math>
\operatorname{PL}(n)\sim \frac{ \zeta(3)^{7/36}}{\sqrt{12\pi}}\ \left(\frac{n}{2}\right)^{-25/36} \ \exp\left(3\ \zeta(3)^{1/3} \left(\frac{n}2\right)^{2/3}+ \zeta'(-1)\right) .
</math>

Evaluating numerically yields

:<math>
\ln \operatorname{PL}(n) \sim 2.00945n^{2/3} -0.69444 \ln n -1.4631.
</math>

=== Plane partitions in a box ===

Around 1896, MacMahon set up the generating function of plane partitions that are subsets of the <math>r \times s \times t</math> box <math>\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)=\{(i,j,k)|1\leq i\leq r, 1\leq j\leq s, 1\leq k\leq t\}
</math> in his first paper on plane partitions.<ref name=":5">{{cite journal|last1=MacMahon|first1=Percy A.|date=1896|title=XVI. Memoir on the theory of the partition of numbers.-Part I|journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences|volume=187|article-number=52}}</ref> The formula is given by
<math display=block> \sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)}q^{|\pi|}=\prod_{i=1}^r\prod_{j=1}^s\frac{1-q^{i+j+t-1}}{1-q^{i+j-1}}
</math>

A proof of this formula can be found in the book ''Combinatory Analysis'' written by MacMahon.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|title=Combinatory Analysis Vol 2|last=MacMahon|first=Major Percy A.|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1916|pages=§495}}</ref> MacMahon also mentions the generating functions of plane partitions.<ref>{{Cite book|last=MacMahon|first=Major Percy A.|date=1916|title=Combinatory Analysis|publisher=Cambridge University Press|volume=2|pages=§429}}</ref> The formula for the generating function can be written in an alternative way, which is given by
<math display=block>
\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)}q^{|\pi|}=\prod_{i=1}^r\prod_{j=1}^s\prod_{k=1}^t\frac{1-q^{i+j+k-1}}{1-q^{i+j+k-2}}
</math>

Multiplying each component by <math>\textstyle\frac{1-q}{1-q}</math>, and setting ''q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 in the formulas above yields that the total number <math>N_1(r, s, t)</math> of plane partitions that fit in the <math>r \times s \times t</math> box <math>\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)</math> is equal to the following product formula:<ref>{{Cite book|title=Combinatory Analysis|last=MacMahon|first=Major Percy A.|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1916|pages=§429,§494}}</ref>
<math display=block>
N_1(r,s,t)=\prod_{(i,j,k)\in \mathcal{B}(r,s,t)}\frac{i+j+k-1}{i+j+k-2}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\frac{i+j+t-1}{i+j-1}.
</math>
The planar case (when ''t'' = 1) yields the [[binomial coefficient]]s:
: <math>\mathcal{B}(r,s,1) = \binom{r+s}{r}.</math>

The general solution is

:<math>\begin{align}
\mathcal{B}(r,s,t) &= \prod_{k=1}^t \frac{(r+s+k-1)!(k-1)!}{(r+k-1)!(s+k-1)!}
\\&= \prod_{k=1}^t \frac{\binom{r+s+k-1}{r+k-1}\binom{r+s+k-1}{s+k-1}}{\binom{r+s+k-1}{r}\binom{s+k-1}{s}}
\end{align}</math>

The [[isometric projection]] of the unit cubes representing a plane partition in a box gives a [[bijection]] between these plane partitions and rhombus tilings of a hexagon with the same edge lengths as the box.<ref name=k94/>

== Special plane partitions ==

Special plane partitions include symmetric, cyclic and self-complementary plane partitions, and combinations of these properties.

In the subsequent sections, the enumeration of special sub-classes of plane partitions inside a box are considered.
These articles use the notation <math>N_i(r,s,t)</math> for the number of such plane partitions, where {{mvar|r}}, {{mvar|s}}, and {{mvar|t}} are the dimensions of the box under consideration, and {{mvar|i}} is the index for the case being considered.

=== Action of ''S''<sub>2</sub>, ''S''<sub>3</sub> and ''C''<sub>3</sub> on plane partitions ===

<math>\mathcal{S}_2</math> is the group of [[Symmetric group|permutations]] acting on the first two coordinates of a point.  This group contains the identity, which sends (''i'', ''j'', ''k'') to itself, and the transposition (''i'', ''j'', ''k'')&nbsp;→&nbsp;(''j'', ''i'', ''k''). The number of elements in an orbit <math>\eta</math> is denoted by <math>|\eta|</math>. <math>\mathcal{B}/\mathcal{S}_2</math> denotes the set of orbits of elements of <math>\mathcal{B}</math> under the action of <math>\mathcal{S}_2</math>. The height of an element (''i'', ''j'', ''k'') is defined by
<math display=block>
ht(i,j,k)=i+j+k-2.
</math>
The height increases by one for each step away from the back right corner. For example, the corner position (1, 1, 1) has height 1 and ''ht''(2, 1, 1) = 2.  The height of an orbit is defined to be the height of any element in the orbit. This notation of the height differs from the notation of [[Ian G. Macdonald]].<ref name=":0" />	

There is a natural action of the permutation group <math>\mathcal{S}_3</math> on a Ferrers diagram of a plane partition—this corresponds to simultaneously permuting the three coordinates of all nodes. This generalizes the conjugation operation for [[integer partition]]s. The action of <math>\mathcal{S}_3</math> can generate new plane partitions starting from a given plane partition. Below there are shown six plane partitions of 4 that are generated by the <math>\mathcal{S}_3</math> action. Only the exchange of the first two coordinates is manifest in the representation given below.
:<math>
\begin{smallmatrix} 3 & 1 \end{smallmatrix} \quad 
\begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \quad
\begin{smallmatrix} 2 &  1 & 1\end{smallmatrix} \quad
\begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1  \end{smallmatrix} \quad 
\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \quad
\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}
</math>

<math>\mathcal{C}_3</math> is called the group of cyclic permutations and consists of

: <math>
(i,j,k)\rightarrow(i,j,k), \quad (i,j,k)\rightarrow(j,k,i), \quad \text{and }\quad (i,j,k)\rightarrow(k,i,j).
</math>

=== Symmetric plane partitions ===

A plane partition <math>\pi</math> is called symmetric if {{pi}}<sub>''i'',''j''</sub> = {{pi}}<sub>''j,i''</sub> for all ''i'', ''j''. In other words, a plane partition is symmetric if <math>(i, j, k)\in \mathcal{B}(r,s,t)</math> if and only if <math>(j, i, k) \in\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)</math>. Plane partitions of this type are symmetric with respect to the plane ''x'' = ''y''. Below is an example of a symmetric plane partition and its visualisation.
[[File:SymmetricPlanePartitions.jpg|thumb|A symmetric plane partition, sum 35]]
: <math> \begin{matrix} 4 &3 &3 &2 &1\\
		      3 &3 &2 &1 &\\
		      3 &2 &2 &1 &\\
		      2 &1 &1 & & \\
		      1 & & & & \end{matrix}
</math>

In 1898, MacMahon formulated his conjecture about the generating function for symmetric plane partitions which are subsets of <math>\mathcal{B}(r,r,t)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=MacMahon|first=Percy Alexander|date=1899|title=Partitions of numbers whose graphs possess symmetry|journal=Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society|volume=17}}</ref> This conjecture is called the '''MacMahon conjecture'''.  The generating function is given by
<math display=block>\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,t)/\mathcal{S}_2}q^{|\pi|}=\prod_{i=1}^r\left[\frac{1-q^{t+2i-1}}{1-q^{2i-1}}\prod_{j=i+1}^r\frac{1-q^{2(i+j+t-1)}}{1-q^{2(i+j-1)}}\right]</math>

Macdonald<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials|last=Macdonald|first=Ian G.|publisher=Clarendon Press|year=1998|isbn=9780198504504|pages=20f, 85f}}</ref> pointed out that Percy A. MacMahon's conjecture reduces to

: <math>\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,t)/\mathcal{S}_2}q^{|\pi|}=\prod_{\eta\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,t)/\mathcal{S}_2}\frac{1-q^{|\eta|(1+ht(\eta))}}{1-q^{|\eta|ht(\eta)}}</math>

In 1972 Edward A. Bender and [[Donald Knuth|Donald E. Knuth]] conjectured<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|author=Bender|author2=Knuth|name-list-style=amp|date=1972|title=Enumeration of plane partitions|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|volume=13|pages=40–54|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(72)90007-6|doi-access=}}</ref> a simple closed form for the generating function for plane partitions which have at most ''r'' rows and strict decrease along the rows. [[George Andrews (mathematician)|George Andrews]] showed<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Andrews|first=George E.|date=1977|title=Plane partitions II: The equivalence of the Bender-Knuth and MacMahon conjectures|journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics|volume=72|issue=2|pages=283–291|doi=10.2140/pjm.1977.72.283|doi-access=free}}</ref> that the conjecture of Bender and Knuth and the MacMahon conjecture are equivalent. MacMahon's conjecture was proven almost simultaneously by George Andrews in 1977<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Andrews|first=George|date=1975|title=Plane Partitions (I): The Mac Mahon Conjecture|journal=Adv. Math. Suppl. Stud.|volume=1}}</ref> and later Ian G. Macdonald presented an alternative proof.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials|last=Macdonald|first=Ian G.|publisher=Clarendon Press|year=1998|isbn=9780198504504|pages=83–86}}</ref> When setting ''q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 yields the counting function <math>N_2(r,r,t)</math> which is given by

: <math>N_2(r,r,t)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\frac{2i+t-1}{2i-1}\prod_{1\leq i< j\leq r}\frac{i+j+t-1}{i+j-1}</math>

For a proof of the case ''q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 please refer to George Andrews' paper ''MacMahon's conjecture on symmetric plane partitions''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Andrews|first=George E.|date=1977|title=MacMahon's conjecture on symmetric plane partitions|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=74|issue=2|pages=426–429|doi=10.1073/pnas.74.2.426|pmid=16592386|pmc=392301|bibcode=1977PNAS...74..426A|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Cyclically symmetric plane partitions ===

{{pi}} is called cyclically symmetric, if the ''i''-th row of <math>\pi</math> is conjugate to the ''i''-th column for all ''i''. The ''i''-th row is regarded as an ordinary partition. The conjugate of a partition <math>\pi</math> is the partition whose diagram is the transpose of partition <math>\pi</math>.<ref name=":0" /> In other words, the plane partition is cyclically symmetric if whenever <math>(i,j,k)\in\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)</math> then (''k'', ''i'', ''j'') and (''j'', ''k'', ''i'') also belong to <math>\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)</math>. Below an example of a cyclically symmetric plane partition and its visualization is given.
[[File:CyclicallySymmetricPlanePartitions M.jpg|thumb|A cyclically symmetric plane partition]]
: <math> \begin{matrix}
	6 &5 &5 &4 &3 &3\\
	6 &4 &3 &3 &1 &\\
	6 &4 &3 &1 &1 &\\
	4 &2 &2 &1 & &\\
	3 &1 &1 & & &\\
	1 &1 &1 & & &
	\end{matrix}
</math>

Macdonald's conjecture provides a formula for calculating the number of cyclically symmetric plane partitions for a given integer ''r''. This conjecture is called the '''Macdonald conjecture'''. The generating function for cyclically symmetric plane partitions which are subsets of <math>\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)</math> is given by

: <math> \sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)/\mathcal{C}_3}q^{|\pi|}=\prod_{\eta\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)/\mathcal{C}_3}\frac{1-q^{|\eta|(1+ht(\eta))}}{1-q^{|\eta|ht(\eta)}}
</math>

This equation can also be written in another way

: <math>\prod_{\eta\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)/\mathcal{C}_3}\frac{1-q^{|\eta|(1+ht(\eta))}}{1-q^{|\eta|ht(\eta)}}=\prod_{i=1}^r\left[\frac{1-q^{3i-1}}{1-q^{3i-2}}\prod_{j=i}^r\frac{1-q^{3(r+i+j-1)}}{1-q^{3(2i+j-1)}}\right]
</math>

In 1979, Andrews proved Macdonald's conjecture for the case ''q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 as the '''"weak" Macdonald conjecture'''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Andrews|first=George E.|date=1979|title=Plane Partitions(III): The Weak Macdonald Conjecture|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|volume=53|issue=3|pages=193–225|doi=10.1007/bf01389763|bibcode=1979InMat..53..193A|s2cid=122528418}}</ref> Three years later William H. Mills, [[David P. Robbins|David Robbins]] and Howard Rumsey proved the general case of Macdonald's conjecture in their paper ''Proof of the Macdonald conjecture''.<ref>{{Cite journal|author1=Mills|author2=Robbins|author3=Rumsey|date=1982|title=Proof of the Macdonald conjecture|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|volume=66|pages=73–88|doi=10.1007/bf01404757|bibcode=1982InMat..66...73M|s2cid=120926391}}</ref> The formula for <math>N_3(r,r,r)</math> is given by the '''"weak" Macdonald conjecture'''

: <math>
N_3(r,r,r)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\left[\frac{3i-1}{3i-2}\prod_{j=i}^r\frac{i+j+r-1}{2i+j-1}\right]
</math>

=== Totally symmetric plane partitions ===

A totally symmetric plane partition <math>\pi</math> is a plane partition which is symmetric and cyclically symmetric. This means that the diagram is symmetric at all three diagonal planes, or in other words that if <math>(i, j, k)\in\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)</math> then all six permutations of (''i'', ''j'', ''k'') are also in <math>\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)</math>. Below an example of a matrix for a totally symmetric plane partition is given. The picture shows the visualisation of the matrix.
[[File:TotalSymmetricPlanePartitions.jpg|thumb|A totally symmetric plane partition]]
: <math> \begin{matrix}	
5 &4 &4 &3 &1\\
4 &3 &3 &1 &\\
4 &3 &2 &1 &\\
3 &1 &1 & & \\
1 & & &&
\end{matrix} 
</math>

Macdonald found the total number of totally symmetric plane partitions that are subsets of <math>\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)</math>. The formula is given by

: <math> N_4(r,r,r)=\prod_{\eta\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)/\mathcal{S}_3}\frac{1+ht(\eta)}{ht(\eta)}
</math>

In 1995 [[John Stembridge|John R. Stembridge]] first proved the formula for <math>N_4(r,r,r)</math><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Stembridge|first=John R.|date=1995|title=The Enumeration of Totally Symmetric Plane Partitions|journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]|volume=111|issue=2|pages=227–243|doi=10.1006/aima.1995.1023|doi-access=free}}</ref> and later in 2005 it was proven by George Andrews, [[Peter Paule]], and Carsten Schneider.<ref>{{Cite journal|author1=Andrews|author2=Paule|author3=Schneider|date=2005|title=Plane Partitions VI: Stembridge's TSPP theorem|journal=Advances in Applied Mathematics|volume=34|issue=4|pages=709–739|doi=10.1016/j.aam.2004.07.008|doi-access=free}}</ref> Around 1983 Andrews and Robbins independently stated an explicit product formula for the orbit-counting generating function for totally symmetric plane partitions.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Proofs and Confirmations|last=Bressoud|first=David M.|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1999|isbn=9781316582756|pages=conj. 13}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Stanley|first=Richard P.|date=1970|title=A Baker's dozen of conjectures concerning plane partitions|journal=Combinatoire énumérative|pages=285–293}}</ref> This formula already alluded to in George E. Andrews' paper ''Totally symmetric plane partitions'' which was published 1980.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Andrews|first=George|date=1980|title=Totally symmetric plane partitions|journal=Abstracts Amer. Math. Soc|volume=1|pages=415}}</ref> The conjecture is called '''The''' '''''q''-TSPP''' '''conjecture''' and it is given by:

Let <math>\mathcal{S}_3</math> be the symmetric group. The orbit counting function for totally symmetric plane partitions that fit inside <math>\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)</math> is given by the formula

: <math> \sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)/\mathcal{S}_3}q^{|\pi|}=\prod_{\eta\in\mathcal{B}(r,r,r)/\mathcal{S}_3}\frac{1-q^{1+ht(\eta)}}{1-q^{ht(\eta)}} = \prod_{1\leq i\leq j\leq k\leq r} \frac{1-q^{i+j+k-1}}{1-q^{i+j+k-2}}.
</math>

This conjecture was proved in 2011 by [[Christoph Koutschan]], [[Manuel Kauers]] and [[Doron Zeilberger]].<ref>{{Cite journal|author1=Koutschan|author2=Kauers|author3=Zeilberger|date=2011|title=A proof of George Andrews' and David Robbins' q-TSPP conjecture|journal=PNAS|volume=108|issue=6|pages=2196–2199|doi=10.1073/pnas.1019186108|pmc=3038772|arxiv=1002.4384|bibcode=2011PNAS..108.2196K|s2cid=12077490|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Self-complementary plane partitions ===

If <math>\pi_{i,j}+\pi_{r-i+1,s-j+1}=t</math> for all <math>1\leq i \leq r</math>, <math>1\leq j \leq s</math>, then the plane partition is called self-complementary. It is necessary that the product <math>r\cdot s\cdot t</math> is even. Below an example of a self-complementary symmetric plane partition and its visualisation is given.
[[File:SelfComplementaryPlanePartition M.jpg|thumb|A self-complementary plane partition]]
: <math> \begin{matrix}
4 &4 &3 &2 &1\\
4 &2 &2 &2 &\\
3 &2 &1 & &
\end{matrix}
</math>

[[Richard P. Stanley]]<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Stanley|first=Richard P.|date=1986|title=Symmetries of Plane Partitions|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|volume=43|pages=103–113|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(86)90028-2|url=http://www-math.mit.edu/~rstan/pubs/pubfiles/65.pdf}}</ref> conjectured formulas for the total number of self-complementary plane partitions <math>N_5(r,s,t)</math>. According to Stanley, Robbins also formulated formulas for the total number of self-complementary plane partitions in a different but equivalent form. The total number of self-complementary plane partitions that are subsets of <math>\mathcal{B}(r,s,t)</math> is given by

: <math> 	N_5(2r,2s,2t)=N_1(r,s,t)^2</math>

: <math> N_5(2r+1,2s,2t)=N_1(r,s,t)N_1(r+1,s,t)</math>

: <math> N_5(2r+1,2s+1,2t)=N_1(r+1,s,t)N_1(r,s+1,t)
</math>

It is necessary that the product of ''r,s'' and ''t'' is even. A proof can be found in the paper ''Symmetries of Plane Partitions'' which was written by Stanley.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1986|title=Erratum|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory|volume=43|pages=310}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> The proof works with Schur functions <math>s_{s^r}(x)</math>. Stanley's proof of the ordinary enumeration of self-complementary plane partitions yields the ''q''-analogue by substituting <math>x_i=q^i</math> for <math>i=1,\ldots,n</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Eisenkölbl|first=Theresia|date=2008|title=A Schur function identity related to the (−1)-enumeration of self complementary plane partitions|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|volume=115|issue=2 |pages=199–212|doi=10.1016/j.jcta.2007.05.004|doi-access=free}}</ref> This is a special case of Stanley's hook-content formula.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Stanley|first=Richard P.|date=1971|title=Theory and Application of Plane Partitions. Part 2|journal=Studies in Applied Mathematics|volume=50|issue=3|pages=259–279|doi=10.1002/sapm1971503259}}</ref> The generating function for self-complementary plane partitions is given by

: <math> s_{\gamma^\alpha}(q,q^2,\ldots,q^n)=q^{\gamma\alpha(\alpha+1)/2}\prod_{i=1}^\alpha \prod_{j=0}^{\gamma-1}\frac{1-q^{i+n-\alpha+j}}{1-q^{i+j}}
</math>

Substituting this formula in

: <math>s_{s^r}(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{t+r})^2 \ \text{ for } \mathcal{B}(2r,2s,2t)</math>

: <math> s_{s^r}(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{t+r}) s_{(s+1)^r}(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{t+r}) \text{ for } \mathcal{B}(2r,2s+1,2t)</math>

: <math> s_{s^{r+1}}(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{t+r+1}) s_{s^r}(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{t+r+1}) \text{ for } \mathcal{B}(2r+1,2s,2t+1)</math>

supplies the desired ''q''-analogue case.

=== Cyclically symmetric self-complementary plane partitions ===

A plane partition <math>\pi</math> is called cyclically symmetric self-complementary if it is [[#Cyclically symmetric plane partitions|cyclically symmetric]] and [[#Self-complementary plane partitions|self-complementary]]. The figure presents a cyclically symmetric self-complementary plane partition and the according matrix is below.
[[File:CyclicallySymmetricSelfCoplementary.jpg|thumb|A cyclically symmetric self-complementary plane partition]]

: <math>\begin{matrix}
4 &4 &4 &1\\
3 &3 &2 &1\\
3 &2 &1 &1\\
3 & & &
\end{matrix}
</math>

In a private communication with Stanley, Robbins conjectured that the total number of cyclically symmetric self-complementary plane partitions is given by <math>N_6(2r,2r,2r)</math>.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> The total number of cyclically symmetric self-complementary plane partitions is given by

: <math> N_6(2r,2r,2r)=D_r^2</math>

<math>D_r</math> is the number of <math>r\times r</math> [[Alternating sign matrix|alternating sign matrices]]. A formula for <math>D_r</math> is given by

: <math> D_r=\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{(3j+1)!}{(r+j)!} </math>

[[Greg Kuperberg]] proved the formula for <math>N_6(r,r,r)</math> in 1994.<ref name=k94>{{Cite journal|last=Kuperberg|first=Greg|date=1994|title=Symmetries of plane partitions and the permanent-determinant method|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|volume=68|pages=115–151|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(94)90094-9|arxiv=math/9410224|bibcode=1994math.....10224K|s2cid=14538036}}</ref>

=== Totally symmetric self-complementary plane partitions ===

A totally symmetric self-complementary plane partition is a plane partition that is both [[#Totally symmetric plane partitions|totally symmetric]] and [[#Self-complementary plane partitions|self-complementary]]. For instance, the matrix below is such a plane partition; it is visualised in the accompanying picture.
[[File:TotallySymmetricSelfCoplementary.jpg|thumb|A totally symmetric self-complementary plane partition]]

: <math>\begin{matrix}
6 &6 &6 &5 &5 &3\\
6 &5 &5 &3 &3 &1\\
6 &5 &5 &3 &3 &1\\
5 &3 &3 &1 &1 & \\
5 &3 &3 &1 &1 & \\
3 &1 &1 & & &
\end{matrix}
</math>

The formula <math>N_7(r,r,r)</math> was conjectured by William H. Mills, Robbins and Howard Rumsey in their work ''Self-Complementary Totally Symmetric Plane Partitions''.<ref>{{Cite journal|author1=Mills|author2=Robbins|author3=Rumsey|date=1986|title=Self-Complementary Totally Symmetric Plane Partitions|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|volume=42|issue=2|pages=277–292|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(86)90098-1|doi-access=}}</ref> The total number of totally symmetric self-complementary plane partitions is given by

: <math> N_7(2r,2r,2r)=D_r </math>

Andrews proved this formula in 1994 in his paper ''Plane Partitions V: The TSSCPP Conjecture''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Andrews|first=George E.|date=1994|title=Plane Partitions V: The TSSCPP Conjecture|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|volume=66|pages=28–39|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(94)90048-5|doi-access=}}</ref>
